sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: AI tutors are most useful when they adapt to each student's strengths, weaknesses, and preferred guidance, but evidence about which guidance works for which student is sparse, slow, and costly to collect from real learners. Student simulators can provide this signal as a proxy, yet existing approaches are limited: state-tracking models fit student behavior but struggle to process explanations or corrections, while LLM role-play follows guidance fluently but does not reliably match the competence of the student being imitated. We present StudentSim, a training framework that turns sparse per-student data into individualized simulators through pooled training followed by per-student specialization. The resulting simulators both mirror a student's own responses and update them under tutor guidance. We also introduce StudentSimEval, a standardized protocol covering 60 students across chess, second-language English writing, and mathematics, using public learner datasets with de-identified records shared for research. StudentSimEval measures behavioral fidelity (F), or how well a simulator matches a student's responses, and guidance responsiveness (R), or how readily it updates under tutor guidance, with all methods fit and evaluated on the same records. Across all three domains, StudentSim outperforms GPT-5.4 on both metrics. In chess, StudentSim reaches F=0.51 and R=0.91, compared with 0.23 and 0.72 for GPT-5.4 and 0.45 and 0.27 for Maia2. As a proof of concept, using StudentSim as a reward model for tutor reinforcement learning produces a chess tutor that expert humans rate as more accurate, better-guided, and more personalized than a no-RL baseline and a tutor trained against a GPT-5.4 simulator reward. Code is available at https://github.com/microsoft/StudentSim.

sections.title: Start
sections.content: StudentSim: Training LLM-based Student Simulators Ke Yang1,2* Chenglong Wang1 Michel Galley1 Chandan Singh1 Jeevana Priya Inala1 ChengXiang Zhai2 Jianfeng Gao1 1Microsoft Research 2University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Abstract AI tutors are most useful when they adaptively respond to each students strengths, weaknesses, and preferred kinds of guidance, but which guidance works for which student is sparse signal, slow and costly to collect from real students. Student simulators can supply that signal as proxy, yet existing ones cover only part of what this requires: state-tracking models fit how student behaves but cannot digest tutors explanations or corrections well, while LLMs prompted to role-play target student follow tutors guidance fluently but do not reliably reproduce the competence of the student they imitate. We present STUDENTSIM, training framework that turns sparse per-student data into an individualized simulator for each student through two-stage pipeline of pooled training followed by per-student specialization, so that the simulator both mirrors the students own responses and updates them under tutor guidance. To measure these two abilities fairly, we build STUDENTSIMEVAL, standardized protocol spanning 60 students across chess, second-language English writing, and mathematics, drawn from public learner datasets whose de-identified student records are shared for research. It scores every method on behavioral fidelity (F ), how well simulator matches students own responses, and guidance responsiveness (R ), how readily it updates its response under tutors guidance, fitting each method on the same records and scoring it on the same held-out records so results are directly comparable; we release our construction and evaluation code so others can score new methods on the same benchmark and extend it. Across all three domains, our per-student simulators outperform GPT-5.4 on both metrics. In chess, for example, STUDENTSIM reaches = 0.51 and = 0.91, compared with 0.23 and 0.72 for GPT-5.4 and 0.45 and 0.27 for Maia2, skill-conditioned chess move prediction model. As proof of concept that the framework also supports AI tutor improvement, trained STUDENTSIM used as the reward for tutor model reinforcement learning yields chess tutor that expert humans rate as more accurate, better-guided, and more personalized than both no-RL baseline and tutor RL-trained against GPT-5.4 simulator reward. Our code is available at https://github.com/microsoft/StudentSim.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: An AI assistant that helps human students learn (e.g., math tutor, foreign-language coach, chess trainer) is more useful when it is trained on real-world interactions across diverse student population: it must see varied backgrounds, baseline skills, and learning styles to understand the typical proficiency and common error patterns of students in that subject, and it must collect feedback on each individuals responses to different teaching materials to learn which teaching approach is most effective for student with particular traits and learning habits. Recruiting and training tutor against such population, however, is prohibitively expensive and time-consuming. Therefore, the evaluation and improvement of adaptive AI tutors lag behind the rapid advancement of the underlying AI models themselves. One alternative is to use student simulators that produce proxy feedback at machine timescales  (Fig. 1)  . Educational measurement assesses learners improvement along two targets: what the learner produces independently, and how far the learner progresses with support, which is the zone of proximal development [VYGOTSKY, 1980] that dynamic assessment operationalizes [Grigorenko and Sternberg, 1998]. Motivated by these, useful simulator must satisfy two requirements  (Fig. 2)  . First, behavioral fidelity: how well the simulator reproduces students own response to problem, including that students characteristic mistakes and strengths. Second, guidance responsiveness: given problem, the students initial response, and tutors guidance addressing it, how readily the simulator updates its response in the direction the guidance is steering. These two axes are the two properties tutor training needs from simulated student, i.e., personalized starting point and the capacity to be taught. pool of such simulators then stands in for diverse population of teachable students for AI tutor training. *Work done during an internship at Microsoft Research. StudentSim: Training LLM-based Student Simulators Existing student simulator approaches usually satisfy only one of these two requirements. State-tracking student models, including knowledge-tracing approaches [Corbett and Anderson, 1995, Piech et al., 2015, Ghosh et al., 2020] and humanstyle behavior prediction models [McIlroyYoung et al., 2020, Tang et al., 2024], are built from real human data and capture aspects of behavioral fidelity, but they have no input pathway for tutor explanations or corrections. Conversely, LLM-prompted user simulators [Owoicho et al., 2023, Terragni et al., 2023] respond to tutor guidance fluently, but even given precise textual description of the students cognitive state, the LLM does not reliably produce behavior consistent with that state. Therefore, the central challenge is to build per-student simulators that are jointly faithful to individual student competence (e.g., their strengths and weaknesses) and responsive to tutor guidance. Figure 1 Real-student feedback is hard to scale; student simulator supplies it at machine timescales. We address this gap with STUDENTSIM, training framework that builds an individualized simulator for each student even though any one student contributes only sparse records. It works in two stages  (Fig. 3)  : first it pools records across all students to pretrain base simulator that captures what is shared in the domain, such as common mistakes and how students revise their responses after guidance; then it specializes that base on single students own records, producing simulator that mirrors that students behavior and updates the way that student would after tutor guidance. To evaluate such simulators on the same footing, we build STUDENTSIMEVAL, standardized protocol spanning 60 students across chess, second-language English writing (L2), and mathematics (math): it turns public learner corpora into fixed per-student record schema with per-student train/held-out splits, and scores every method on two metrics, behavioral fidelity (F) and guidance responsiveness (R). Because every method is fit on the same per-student records and scored on the same held-out records under the same metrics, STUDENTSIMEVAL makes per-student simulators directly comparable, whether they come from our framework or from prior families. Applying our training framework yields reference family of 60 STUDENTSIM simulators. The learner corpora are public, and we release the construction (a) What simulator is scored on (b) Where each method lands, on chess Figure 2 Scoring student simulator. Education tracks learners progress through what they produce independently and how far they advance once support arrives, the zone of proximal development [VYGOTSKY, 1980] that dynamic assessment operationalizes [Grigorenko and Sternberg, 1998]. We score whether student simulator can serve as feedback source for tutor, which rests on two abilities mirroring those signals: behavioral fidelity, behaving like the student it stands for, and guidance responsiveness, moving where the tutors guidance indicates (a). On chess (b), STUDENTSIM leads on both, the prompted LLM on responsiveness alone, and the state-tracking model on fidelity alone, and the same ranking holds in L2 and math (Table 2 and Table 3). 2 StudentSim: Training LLM-based Student Simulators pipeline, per-student splits, and evaluation code so others can score new methods on STUDENTSIMEVAL and extend it. Across all three domains the reference simulators outperform GPT-5.4 [OpenAI, 2026], strong closed-sourced LLM prompted to role-play students, on both behavioral fidelity and guidance responsiveness, both on average and on most individual students. For example, in chess, STUDENTSIM reaches = 0.51 and = 0.91, compared with = 0.23 and = 0.72 for GPT-5.4 and = 0.45 and = 0.27 for Maia2 [Tang et al., 2024], skill-conditioned chess move-prediction model that stands in for the state-tracking family. The results show that each baseline is weak on different axis: GPT-5.4 follows tutor guidance fluently, which earns it fair R, but prompting alone cannot make it reproduce particular students competence and mistakes, so its stays low. Maia2 is trained on real human games and tracks players move distribution reasonably well, earning moderate F, but it has no input pathway for natural-language guidance and stays near its zero-instruction floor, so its collapses. STUDENTSIM is the only model strong on both axes. The same pattern holds in L2 and math, with full per-domain numbers in Sections 5.2 and 5.3. We also give proof of concept that connects student simulation back to AI tutor improvement. Using trained STUDENTSIM as the reward model for chess tutor reinforcement learning produces an AI tutor that expert human raters score as more accurate, better-guided, and more personalized than both the supervised-finetuned starting tutor with no RL and tutor RL-trained against GPT-5.4 student-simulator reward (Sec. 6). We do not present this as best-tutor claim, but as evidence that trained student simulators can provide useful, practical proxy feedback for AI tutor optimization. In sum, our contributions are: i) we present the first framework to cast personalized student simulation as concrete target for AI tutor optimization, jointly formalizing the two properties simulator must have, behavioral fidelity (F) and guidance responsiveness (R); this F/R decomposition is what turns student simulation into an optimizable objective; ii) STUDENTSIM, which overcomes sparse per-student data through pooled training and per-student specialization to realize both properties; iii) STUDENTSIMEVAL, standardized protocol over 60 students in chess, L2 English writing, and math, with released code, under which our reference family of simulators outperforms state-tracking and prompted-LLM baselines; and iv) chess tutor reinforcement-learning proof of concept in which trained STUDENTSIM reward yields the best-rated AI tutor in an expert human study.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: We organize prior work on student simulation and AI tutor optimization into three lines. First, cognitive-state and behavior-prediction models, including knowledge tracing and human-play move predictors, match learner behavior at the population level but have no input channel for natural-language guidance [Corbett and Anderson, 1995, Piech et al., 2015, Ghosh et al., 2020, McIlroy-Young et al., 2020, Tang et al., 2024]. Second, LLM-prompted student and user simulators are conditioned on textual descriptions and engage with conversational text [Owoicho et al., 2023, Terragni et al., 2023]; this recipe has been instantiated across educational settings as dialogue-tutoring corpora, multi-agent classrooms, application-specific simulators, and learner-data generation [Macina et al., 2023, Zhang et al., 2024, Gao et al., 2026, Xu et al., 2025, 2024, Lu and Wang, 2024, Markel et al., 2023]. Competence description alone is, however, only thin conditioning channel, and growing validity-focused literature raises concerns about LLM-prompted simulators from architectural, fidelity-benchmark, and teacher-facing angles [Yuan et al., 2026, Scarlatos et al., 2026, Wu et al., 2025, Martynova et al., 2025, Mannekote et al., 2024, Louie et al., 2024, Peng and Shang, 2024, Samuel et al., 2025, Wang et al., 2024c]. Third, tutor-side work supervises tutor explanations on expert-curated dialogues [Chevalier et al., 2024] or queries generic LLM judge against quality rubric [Zheng et al., 2023]; recent attempts to ground the tutors reward in rubric-judge feedback or simulated-student use knowledge-tracing model or prompted LLM student rather than simulator trained on real learner data [Scarlatos et al., 2025b, Dinucu-Jianu et al., 2025, Maurya et al., 2025], while parallel tutor-side line builds pedagogical evaluation benchmarks and runs classroom or expert-preference studies of tutor models [Macina et al., 2025, Wang et al., 2025, 2024b, Team et al., 2025]. To our knowledge, STUDENTSIM is the first to i) formalize per-student simulation as measurable target defined jointly by behavioral fidelity and guidance responsiveness; ii) train per-student simulators on real per-individual learner data that both match students own behavior and respond to natural-language tutor guidance; and iii) use such trained simulator as the reward source for optimizing an AI tutor (Sec. 6). Sec. gives the per-strand survey with methodological detail. 3 StudentSim: Training LLM-based Student Simulators

sections.title: 3 Problem Formulation
sections.content: Let {π1, . . . , πN } be real students and {M1, . . . , MN } be trained student simulators, where Mi is meant to approximate πi. For each student i, we hold out two kinds of recorded data. Single-turn records, Si = {(x, m)}, pair problem with the students actual response m; Si serves to measure whether the simulators prediction matches the students response. Multi-turn records, Ti = {(x, m, τ, m)}, additionally include the tutor guidance τ provided to address the students wrong response on and the canonical corrected response that the guidance is steering toward (e.g., the engine-recommended move in chess, the corrected fragment in second-language English writing, or the correct answer in mathematics); Ti serves to measure whether the simulator successfully updates toward after reading guidance. useful population must answer two questions: does each simulator match its target students behavior on Si, and does it produce the corrected response on Ti after reading guidance? Behavioral fidelity. Per-student behavioral fidelity, Fi, scores simulator Mi on Si: how well its response on held-out problem matches student πis recorded response. Each of three domains tested in STUDENTSIMEVAL instantiates this match notion to its own response space. In chess, fidelity is move-prediction accuracy: how often the simulators predicted move is the same move the student actually played. In second-language English writing, fidelity is error-profile match: whether the simulators generated essay matches the students overall error rate and issue-type profile. In mathematics, where problems are four-way multiple-choice, fidelity is how faithfully the simulators prediction matches the option the student actually selected. The population score is = 1 Fi. Appendix gives the per-benchmark formula and operational recipe; Appendix F.3 gives the design rationale for the per-domain operationalization. (cid:80) Guidance responsiveness. Per-student guidance responsiveness, Ri, scores simulator Mi on Ti using multi-turn records (x, m, τ, m), where is the problem, is the students initial response, τ is the tutor guidance addressing it, and is the response that guidance is steering toward. Ri asks: after reading (x, m, τ ), does the simulator update to m? The population score is = 1 Ri. This isolates the simulators update under guidance: behavioral fidelity already captures the student-specific answer patterns present before the intervention, and captures whether the simulator takes up the guidance and follows it to the endpoint it steers toward. That is the operative property when the simulator serves as reward model for tutor training (Section 6), since static imitator that ignores guidance offers no signal about whether an intervention moved the student. Appendix F.1 details this target choice. (cid:80) Orthogonality. and measure separable capabilities: faithful but unresponsive simulator describes the student without responding to guidance, and responsive but unfaithful one follows guidance from the wrong starting state. Therefore, the high-F, high-R corner is the target.

sections.title: 4 StudentSim Training Pipeline
sections.content: Each student in the populations we study contributes only small amount of recorded data. For example, learner in the second-language English writing corpus [Öksüz et al., 2025] writes three essays at the median, and more than two thirds write five or fewer (Appendix B). This sparsity is not specific to our setup: collecting records from real users is slow and costly, and assembling per-user data on this order typically takes months to years of collection, so per-user data sparsity is familiar problem in any system that learns from interactions with real users [Schein et al., 2002, Lee et al., 2019, Bhattacharjee and Wayllace, 2025, Li et al., 2017]. It is also problem that data-hungry large language models are particularly poorly equipped to solve directly: training one simulator end-to-end per student from small per-student record would overfit, and would also have to relearn the shared structure of student behavior in the domain from scratch every time [Dodge et al., 2020, Finn et al., 2017]. We therefore train each per-student simulator in two stages  (Fig. 3)  . Stage 1: pooled training. Stage 1 trains one domain-specific base simulator on data pooled across all students in the domain. This stage learns what is shared across students: common mistake patterns, the response format expected in the domain, and the pathway from natural-language tutor guidance to changed response. The output of Stage 1 is one base simulator per domain that already exhibits broad student-like behavior but has not yet been specialized to any individual student. Stage 2: per-student specialization. Stage 2 initializes from the Stage 1 base simulator and adapts it to one specific student using only that students own recorded responses and recorded tutor-guidance interactions. Each student receives 4 StudentSim: Training LLM-based Student Simulators Figure 3 Two-stage training pipeline for STUDENTSIM. Stage 1 pools the sparse records of many students in domain and trains one base simulator on what they share. Stage 2 specializes that base to single student on that students own records, yielding one simulator per student. an independent specialization, producing one simulator Mi per student. Stage 2 captures what is specific to the individual student: for example, which mistakes particular student tends to make, and how that students behavior shifts in response to given form of tutor guidance. Why two stages. Stage 1 supplies what is shared across students and what cannot be learned reliably from one students sparse data alone; for example, in chess, performance drops when pooled records are replaced with repeated records from one student (Appendix D.1). Stage 2 supplies what is specific to each individual student.

sections.title: 5 Results
sections.content: This section instantiates the framework on chess, second-language English writing (L2), and mathematics (math). Sec. 5.1 specifies data sources, tasks, guidance types, training setup, and baselines. Sec. 5.2 reports behavioral fidelity F. Sec. 5.3 reports guidance responsiveness R.

sections.content: Data sources, tasks, and student populations. Each domain provides single-turn records (problem student response) used to learn students baseline behavior and multi-turn records (problem wrong response tutor guidance canonical corrected response) used to learn how student updates after tutor guidance, instantiating the (Si, Ti) schema from Sec. 3. All three corpora consist of records from real human students. For chess, the corpus is drawn from Lichess (May 2025), fully open-source online chess platform on which players record real games against human opponents; each record pairs board position with the players actual move. The simulator task is to predict specific players next move and their response to natural-language coach guidance. For second-language English writing (L2), we use the EFCAMDAT corpus [Geertzen et al., 2013], collection of essays by English-as-foreign-language learners alongside tutor corrections; the simulator task is to generate essays whose error patterns match specific learner, and to predict the learners response after tutor correction. Construction of the multi-turn corpora (real-teacher-annotated for L2, controllable LLM-tutor-generated for chess and math under fixed style templates) is detailed in Appendix F.2; for chess and math, the LLM determines only the wording of the guidance, while the response it steers toward is fixed in advance by the engine or an audited answer key. Guidance types. Effective tutoring adjusts the level of support to what the learner needs at that moment, giving more when the student is struggling and stepping back as the student takes over [Wood et al., 1976]. Each domain therefore includes guidance types that span that range of support: chess uses error remediation (diagnosing the error and explaining the correction), comparative (contrasting the played move with stronger alternatives), strategic (outlining the plan the chess position calls for), and Socratic (asking questions that guide the students reasoning); L2 uses point-based (scoping feedback to one error occurrence) and rule-based (explaining the underlying grammatical rule) correction; math uses error remediation, Socratic, and conceptual explanation (teaching the principle behind the error). Error remediation covers the direct-correction end of that range, the appropriate tutor action when learner is stuck or repeatedly failing [Koedinger and Aleven, 2007]. tutor trained against the simulator has to learn when to use that level of support, so the training environment must include students who respond to it. At the other end, Socratic and conceptual modes correspond to the case where the tutor asks questions or supplies principle without stating which response is correct, so the learner must work the correction out for themselves. The simulated student must then reason through those hints to arrive at the correction, making these modes the hardest case for guidance responsiveness. Multi-turn records mix these guidance types uniformly during training so the simulator learns to follow any of them at evaluation time; per-mode breakdown is in Appendix C.7. Training setup. The base model in all three domains is Qwen3-4B-Instruct [Yang et al., 2025]. Stage 1 trains one domain-specific LoRA adapter on records pooled across the Stage-1 student set, mixing single-turn and multi-turn records at multi-turn ratio of 0.2. Single-turn records train fidelity, multi-turn records train guidance responsiveness, and joint training develops both. Stage 2 continues training the Stage-1 adapter on each Stage-2 students own records, producing one specialized adapter per student. This two-stage design separates the learning of population-level behavior patterns (Stage 1, pooled training across all students) from per-student specialization (Stage 2), so each students adapter refines well-initialized shared foundation rather than training from scratch on sparse individual data. An ablation of this two-stage design is given in Appendix D.1. Both stages share the base model, LoRA architecture, and optimizer; the small number of per-domain differences in batch size and optimization length follow directly from each domains dataset scale, with all other settings held identical across domains. Decoding is greedy (T = 0). Headline numbers in Sections 5.25.3 are the cross-seed mean over 3 independent training runs; run-to-run standard deviations are in Appendix E.4. sections.title: 5.3 Guidance Responsiveness Results
sections.content: Across all three domains, the trained simulators outperform every baseline on aggregate  (Table 3)  ; the gap is largest on the open-ended guidance modes, where the tutor prompts the student to reason toward the fix through questions or principles. higher also has different concrete meaning per benchmark: in chess, after reading the tutors textual guidance the simulator switches from its initial wrong move to corrected move that the guidance is steering it toward; in L2, after reading the teachers feedback, which flags the offending fragment of an essay, the simulator supplies the exact correction that fragment requires; in math, after the tutor walks the student through the reasoning behind their error, the simulators ability to revise its initial wrong numerical answer to the correct one improves. The case study below illustrates this on the strictest of the chess modes. Fig. 5 examines the strictest of the four chess guidance modes, Socratic. Here the tutor leads the student toward the fix through chain of questions and does not state the corrected move, so the simulator must infer the canonical correction from that reasoning. The position is held out from both pooled training and per-player training. The players actual move is the pawn push 1.g5g6, serious blunder; the engine best move is the queen check f8b4. The Socratic prompt asks the student to compare the pawn push with forcing queen move that gives check from the queenside. The prompt never names the destination square; the model has to derive the answer from the chain of guiding questions. The baselines fail in three different ways. Maia2 has no input pathway for natural-language guidance and reproduces the players blunder. GPT-5.4 reads the prompt and selects queen move, but answers different wrong square (f8f4). Our per-player simulator, 4B Qwen3 base with single per-player LoRA adapter, reasons through the same chain 8 StudentSim: Training LLM-based Student Simulators Figure 6 Tutor RL with frozen student simulator as the reward source. Each episode replays real students wrong answer, the tutor policy proposes guidance, the frozen simulator revises, and the improvement in move quality drives the RL update. of questions and outputs the engine best move f8b4. That 4B trained simulator solves the Socratic case where prompted access to much larger closed-source model fails is direct evidence that the multi-turn training stage adds guidance-following capability, not merely hint-copying shortcut on the easy modes where the prompt already contains the answer. Per-mode breakdowns by guidance type are in Appendix C.7.

sections.title: 6 Tutor RL with Student Simulator Feedback
sections.content: This section gives chess proof of concept that our trained STUDENTSIM, used as the reward model for tutor reinforcement learning, produces better tutor than two natural alternatives: the supervised-finetuned tutor with no RL, and reward in which frontier LLM (GPT-5.4) plays the student simulator. We keep this proof of concept: the claim is that faithful, responsive student simulator is useful and practical reward signal for AI tutor optimization, not that we produce best-in-class tutor. Chess is the right scope because it admits precise per-position reward (Stockfish [The Stockfish developers, 2025] centipawn evaluation) that decouples the validation signal from the simulators behavior; transfer to other domains needs per-domain reward functions on free-form responses, outside the claim tested here (Appendix F.6). We evaluate all conditions with an expert human study (Appendix E.5). Setup. The loop is shown in Fig. 6. Each episode draws chess problem and the students recorded wrong move Aprev from real student records; the tutor proposes guidance, frozen student simulator emits revised move Arev, and the reward rewards guidance that improves move quality, derived from precomputed Stockfish lookup of Arev relative to Aprev (full formulation in Appendix E). All conditions share the same tutor policy (Qwen3-VL-8B [Bai et al., 2025]), which reads the position as rendered board alongside the text, and the same SFT starting point, optimized with GRPO [Shao et al., 2024]; they differ only in the reward model: No RL: the SFT tutor itself, lower-bound control. GPT-5.4 simulator: the reward uses GPT-5.4 prompted to play the student; GPT-5.4 emits the revised move after reading the tutors guidance, and the shared move-quality reward scores that move. This is the heavyweight, closed, fixed-behavior baseline that depends on frontier-model API at every rollout. STUDENTSIM (Ours): the reward is our trained STUDENTSIM together with two extensible reward heads mounted on the same simulator backbone, both reading the tutors explanation. The frozen-simulator term is the shared move-quality improvement of the simulators revised move; personalization head scores whether the explanation follows the intended teaching style; and perception head penalizes explanations that misdescribe the board, such as naming wrong square or hallucinated piece. The two heads act as multiplicative gates on the move-quality term (Appendix E.5). The simulator and heads are small, open, and served locally, and the head set can be customized to the student role one wants to optimize against. Our reward uses the pooled Stage-1 STUDENTSIM simulator, which captures population-level student behavior, so the tutor is optimized to improve guidance for students in general and the reward is not tied to any single individuals idiosyncrasies. 9 StudentSim: Training LLM-based Student Simulators Expert Human Study. After tutor model optimization, competitive chess players rate each tutors generated guidance, blind to presentation order, on three axes: accuracy (the fraction of tutors responses with no misleading factual error), guidance quality (a 15 rating of how well the response teaches), and personalization (a 15 rating in the context of Socratic-leaning student). Among the rewards we study, our STUDENTSIM reward produces the best-rated tutor on all three axes  (Table 4)  . The GPT-5.4-simulator reward stays below even the no-RL baseline on accuracy, held back by markedly higher rate of severe factual errors. Full study details are in Appendix E.5. Table 4 Human evaluation of the AI chess tutors. Accuracy is the percentage of responses with no actively misleading factual error; guidance and personalization are 15 ratings. Scores are means over the studys 74 annotations from 8 annotators. The triply-annotated and 2000+ elo expert subsets in Appendix E.5 give the same ordering. Condition Accuracy (%) Guidance (15, ) Personalization (15, ) No RL GPT-5.4 reward STUDENTSIM (Ours) 75.7 71.6 90.5 2.99 3.08 3.31 2.80 2.42 3.93 Scope and interpretation. The comparison isolates the reward model: all three conditions share the tutor policy, the SFT start, and the GRPO setup, so the differences trace to the reward. The style and perception heads are only lightweight linear probes; they work because they read our trained simulators own backbone, which already encodes student behavior and board state. closed frontier-model API used as the simulator exposes no such backbone to probe, so it admits no comparable heads. The trained student simulator is thus the source of the signal in both roles: it produces the faithful, responsive move-level reward, and its backbone is what the heads extend to score the tutors factual grounding and teaching style. The human-study gains across all three axes therefore follow from single trained student simulator, evidence that faithful, responsive simulator makes the reward practically effective for AI tutor optimization.

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: STUDENTSIM is training framework for per-student AI student simulation built around two requirements that must hold together: behavioral fidelity (F), how well simulator matches students own responses, and guidance responsiveness (R), how reliably it updates towards where the tutor guidance leads. To measure both abilities on common footing, STUDENTSIMEVAL casts public learner corpora for research across chess, second-language English writing, and mathematics into standardized per-student protocol on which any simulator, from our framework or prior family, is fit and scored on the same held-out records. Under this protocol, STUDENTSIMs two-stage pooled-then-specialized pipeline yields reference family of 60 individualized simulators that are strong on both axes across all three domains, outperforming domain-specific state-tracking (weak on R) and prompt-only LLM role-play (weak on F). As proof of concept that trained simulator can also drive AI tutor improvement, frozen STUDENTSIM used as the reward in chess tutor RL loop yields tutor that expert humans rate as more accurate, better-guided, and more personalized than tutors trained with frontier-LLM-simulator reward or the baseline model with no RL. Looking ahead, behavioral fidelity and guidance responsiveness capture students state and its one-step update under guidance. Reproducing the fuller learning dynamics student shows over time, how they acquire, retain, and forget knowledge across many student-tutor interactions or even through self-learning, is the deeper foundation of simulators value for AI tutor optimization and the direction STUDENTSIM opens toward.

sections.title: A Related Work
sections.content: This appendix expands Section 2 with per-paper survey along the same three lines: cognitive-state and behaviorprediction models (Sec. A.1), LLM-prompted student simulators (Sec. A.2), and tutor-side evaluation and optimization (Sec. A.3). A.1 Cognitive-State and Behavior-Prediction Models Knowledge tracing. Knowledge tracing infers students latent cognitive state from sequence of observed responses and predicts future responses. Bayesian Knowledge Tracing maintains per-skill Bernoulli mastery variable updated after each attempt with four parameters (prior, learn, slip, guess) [Corbett and Anderson, 1995]; Deep Knowledge Tracing replaces hand-specified updates with recurrent network over the interaction history [Piech et al., 2015]; attentive variants condition on items and recent context for longer-range and item-similarity effects [Ghosh et al., 2020]. Related state representations include key-value memory and transformer KT, auxiliary-task DKT, Item Response Theory and multidimensional IRT, and performanceand learning-factor analysis [Zhang et al., 2017, Pandey and Karypis, 2019, Choi et al., 2020, Liu et al., 2023, Lord, 2012, Reckase, 1985, I. et al., 2009, Cen et al., 2006]. Across the family the state is compact latent updated from labeled response outcomes (correct/incorrect, sometimes latency, partial credit, or hints used), and the prediction target is the next items outcome; the observation channel never includes free-form tutor guidance. LLM-based knowledge tracing. From 2024 onward, question text and dialogue enter the KT stack. Integrating pretrained language-model representations of question text improves cold-start generalization over item-id baselines [Lee et al., 2024]; extending KT to tutor-student dialogues with per-turn skill and correctness annotation beats classical KT especially under limited data [Scarlatos et al., 2025a]; and uncertainty-aware variants add stochastic-embedding uncertainty [Cheng et al., 2025]. The dialogue-KT entry is the closest published prior art for our axis, being the only KT variant that ingests tutor language as input, yet all of these predict answer correctness from one shared model rather than generating specific students responses from per-student one. From correctness prediction to response generation. Option Tracing predicts which distractor student selects rather than only whether they answer correctly [Ghosh et al., 2021]; Open-Ended KT extends the idea to free-form responses in programming tasks, predicting the exact response rather than its correctness label, and is the canonical precursor of STUDENTSIMs response-generation objective [Liu et al., 2022]. Human behavior cloning in chess. parallel strand fits behavioral predictors directly to logs of human play. Maia trains separate move-prediction network for each rating band and reproduces characteristic human mistakes at the target skill level, best predicting the blunders human players make [McIlroy-Young et al., 2020]; Maia2 extends it into single skill-conditioned network with stronger prediction and broader rating coverage [Tang et al., 2024]. Maia2 is closer to population-level behavior cloning at target skill than to per-skill state tracking, but shares the same conditioning limit: small structured descriptor (rating, history, sometimes time control), no free-form text, and no per-individual fit. Where the gap shows up. This whole line updates state only from labeled outcomes, has no architectural route by which paragraph of explanation, hint, or worked example becomes an update to the latent, and is fit population-wide. Under our metrics it clears at or above untrained-LLM baselines (e.g., on chess, Maia2 is the strongest baseline; Section 5.2), but its collapses to near-zero, zero-instruction floor because guidance text has no input pathway (Section 5.3). A.2 LLM-Prompted Student Simulators User and student simulation. second strand prompts large language model to role-play target user: build textual description of the target (preferences, knowledge state, persona), prepend it to the conversation, and let the model continue conditioned on it. This recipe is used to evaluate conversational and task-oriented dialogue agents by replaying simulated user turns [Owoicho et al., 2023, Terragni et al., 2023], and recurs as persona prompting, profile-conditioned simulation, synthetic-user generation for offline evaluation, and interactive goal-directed simulation, sometimes constrained with in-context exemplars or dual-LLM coordination [Luo et al., 2024]. parallel line measures whether such role-plays stay consistent with described character, using the resulting scores as benchmarks, as training 17 StudentSim: Training LLM-based Student Simulators data, or as rewards for fine-tuning persona-following [Peng and Shang, 2024, Samuel et al., 2025, Wang et al., 2024c, Jiang et al., 2024, Wang et al., 2024a, Shao et al., 2023, Tu et al., 2024, Gusev, 2025]. Critical observation. The simulator is frozen LLM with prompt, pretrained to generate plausible language rather than to map description of learner onto the behavioral consequences of that cognitive state. Two failure modes follow: the simulator solves problems beyond the described students level, or its surface mimicry overshoots and misses problems the student would solve. Both appear in our chess data, where GPT-5.4 reaches = 0.23 and GPT-4o = 0.22, below state-tracking baselines, even as they attain higher than state-tracking models can (Section 5.2). We classify any system whose output is student-style response (an answer, an essay, confusion message) as student simulator, and reserve judge or LLM-as-judge for systems whose output is scalar score or rubric verdict [Zheng et al., 2023]; the proxy-reward and LLM-as-judge line lives in Sec. A.3. A.2.1 Student-Simulation Validity The validity of LLM-based student simulation has emerged as an open question. The competence paradox holds that broadly capable LLM asked to behave as partially knowledgeable learner produces fluent but unreliable student text, because its pretrained reasoning and helpfulness habits override the competence description; this line reframes simulator validity as constrained generation under an explicit epistemic-state specification, with state evolution under instruction as required axis rather than an emergent side effect of prompting [Yuan et al., 2026]. Empirical work measures simulated-student quality directly and reports systematic mismatches with real students in solve rate and error type [Scarlatos et al., 2026], and other work proposes architectural changes such as cognitive prototype modules or controlled imperfect reasoning to elicit student-like errors instead of correcting them away [Wu et al., 2025]. Teacher-facing studies add that instructors find LLM students overly attentive, emotionally flat, linguistically too sophisticated, and inconsistent across turns [Martynova et al., 2025]. Our axis targets exactly this per-individual fidelity gap: each simulator is trained against real learners behavioral data and scored per student on held-out records that learner produced. R, by contrast, scores whether the simulator produces the canonical corrected response under tutor guidance (Appendix F.1), which is what tutor RL loop rewards: guidance that moves the student to the right answer. How closely tracks an individual students literal post-guidance behavior is complementary, counterfactual question that controlled studies with real students under matched guidance can address, natural extension of the metric. A.2.2 Educational Student Simulators Educational simulators instantiate the prompting recipe in several ways: half-synthetic tutoring dialogues from teacher LLM-student pairing or crowdworker role-play [Macina et al., 2023, Stasaski et al., 2020]; multi-agent classrooms and generative learner agents with reflective memory, class-control mechanisms, or longitudinal real-student datasets [Zhang et al., 2024, Gao et al., 2026, Xu et al., 2025]; profileand personality-conditioned simulators tying behavior to cognitive-ability and personality traits [Liu et al., 2024b]; and application-driven simulators for item-quality evaluation, teaching-assistant training, and learner-data generation [Lu and Wang, 2024, Markel et al., 2023, Xu et al., 2024]. per-individual sub-line specifies agents per target rather than per group: patient-simulation elicits per-target naturallanguage behavioral principles for prompted LLM, the closest per-individual specification methodology even though it is prompt-based and non-educational [Louie et al., 2024], and social-science work constructs per-individual agents from persons self-reports, builds generative agents with retrieval-based memory, or equips LLM agents with task-agnostic plugin memory modules, using prompting, retrieval, and external memory rather than weight specialization and without evaluating state evolution under instruction [Park et al., 2026, 2023, Yang et al., 2026]. These approaches vary along granularity (persona, profile, group, or individual), conditioning interface (prompt, prompt-plus-retrieval, or weight-level fine-tuning), and evaluation target (stylistic plausibility, downstream task, or response-level fidelity to specific learner); STUDENTSIM is per-individual, weight-level, and response-level with the additional guidance-response axis, combination we are not aware of in prior educational work. A.3 Tutor-Side Evaluation and Optimization Tutor models, judges, and benchmarks. The third line studies the AI tutor side of the loop. Tutor-specialized models supervise on expert-curated or synthetic tutoring dialogues [Chevalier et al., 2024]; proxy-reward and LLM-as-judge methods supply scalar feedback by querying generic LLM against quality rubric, with the target being rubric quality or human preference rather than specific students response [Zheng et al., 2023]. Benchmark work moves 18 StudentSim: Training LLM-based Student Simulators from single-rubric judges toward multi-dimensional pedagogical evaluation and documents tension between tutor models subject expertise and its pedagogical skill [Macina et al., 2025, Maurya et al., 2025]. Classroom-scale studies test tutor-assist and tutor-as-replacement settings against real students and report learning gains, in some cases with particular benefit to under-served populations [Wang et al., 2025], and LLM-tutor instruction-tuning reports parallel pedagogical-quality gains under expert preference evaluation [Team et al., 2025]. separate line conditions tutor output on student descriptor or structured pedagogical strategy (a profile, recent error, an instructional style, or step-by-step scaffolding) [Sonkar et al., 2023, Nye et al., 2014, Liu et al., 2024a], extending the intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) lineage exemplified by Squirrel AI, ALEKS, and Carnegie Learning; STUDENTSIM differs from ITS-era student models in handling open-ended natural-language guidance and training per individual rather than fitting small skill graph with hand-coded production rules. Simulator-grounded rewards. The closest cluster to our downstream setup uses knowledge-tracing model or prompted LLM student as the reward signal in tutor optimization loop rather than generic rubric. One pattern scores candidate tutor utterances by knowledge-tracing models predicted post-turn correctness, combines that with rubric judge, and trains the tutor via direct preference optimization [Scarlatos et al., 2025b]; another runs full online RL loop in which the tutor and prompted LLM student converse for multiple turns and the tutor is rewarded by the simulated students post-dialogue solve rate plus pedagogy judge, optimized via GRPO [Dinucu-Jianu et al., 2025]. What recurs across this cluster is that the reward is grounded in knowledge-tracing model that predicts only answer correctness or prompted LLM student, rather than simulator trained on real student behavioral data; where the student is prompted LLM, the model that judges its simulated learner is typically the same generic LLM, so the reward is only as well-grounded as that LLMs persona-following, which the validity literature in Sec. A.2.1 documents to be unstable. Section 6 supplies the missing pathway: frozen STUDENTSIM, trained on real learner data and calibrated on and R, is plugged into tutor RL loop as the reward source, with the reward depending on whether the simulated students response improves under tutor guidance (r = score(Arev) score(Aprev)). Because the signal is grounded in real-learner-derived behavior rather than prompted persona or generic rubric, expert raters judge the resulting tutor as more accurate, better-guided, and more personalized than tutors rewarded by prompted-simulator reward or no reinforcement learning (Sec. 6). Per-Benchmark Data and Tasks This appendix documents the source corpus, raw record fields, training-instance formats, and corpus-level statistics for each of the three domains the STUDENTSIM framework instantiates. Each subsection follows the same fiveblock structure: data source, raw record, single-turn record format Si = {(x, m)}, multi-turn record format Ti = {(x, m, τ, m)}, and corpus-statistics tabular. Symbols Si and Ti are defined in Section 3. Worked examples below show real fields with identifiers anonymized as Player (chess) or Student (second-language English writing and mathematics). B.1 The STUDENTSIMEVAL Evaluation Protocol STUDENTSIMEVAL fixes, once and independently of any method, both the population of evaluated students and the per-student held-out records that every method is scored on. It evaluates frozen roster of 30 chess players, 15 L2 learners, and 15 math students (60 in total). For each student it fixes two held-out sets, disjoint from all training data: single-turn set Si that scores behavioral fidelity F, and multi-turn set Ti that scores guidance responsiveness R. The split is chronological: each students earlier records form the training pool and their later records are held out for Si and Ti, so every score reflects prediction of students later behavior from their earlier records. Every method, our trained simulators and the GPT-4o, GPT-5.4, Maia2, and base-Qwen baselines alike, is fit on the same per-student training records and scored on these same held-out sets. The held-out sets are materialized once as frozen split files and reused verbatim, so they are property of the protocol, not of any method; new method is evaluated by running it on the same files. The per-student held-out sizes are the Held-out columns of Table 1: Si = 5,000 and Ti = 4,000 in chess; Si = 26 and Ti = 40 in L2; Si = 66 in math, with Ti ranging over 21 to 99. The multi-turn set is split evenly across each domains guidance modes: four in chess (error remediation, comparative, strategic, Socratic), two in L2 (point-based, rule-based), and three in math (error remediation, Socratic, conceptual). The protocol equalizes the number of held-out records per student wherever the data allows, so that no student dominates population mean. Where domain has more records than the budget needs, cap gives every student the same count; 19 StudentSim: Training LLM-based Student Simulators where equalizing would leave too little to estimate the metric, the protocol keeps every available record instead. Chess uses an absolute cap of 5,000 single-turn positions and 1,000 multi-turn records per guidance mode, subsampled so every player contributes the same count from larger available pool. For the scarcer single-turn data in L2 and math, we equalize to the smallest students held-out size, giving Si = 26 (L2) and Si = 66 (math) for every student, and L2 caps its multi-turn set at 20 records per correction mode. Math multi-turn records are the case where equalizing would leave too little to estimate R, since multi-turn record exists only for problem the student first answered incorrectly, so the protocol keeps every eligible wrong-answer problem, fanned across the three guidance modes (879 records in total, 293 per mode). Training draws separate capped subset of each students records, so the held-out portion is reserved and never enters any training stage. B.2 Chess Data source. The chess records come from the public Lichess game-database export at https://database.lichess.org/ [Lichess, 2025], specifically the May 2025 monthly snapshot of standard-time-control human games. Lichess is an open-source online chess platform on which every published game is between two real human players; no game in the export is engine-vs-engine or otherwise synthetic. The platform also publishes Stockfish position evaluations for many games, and our pipeline uses these where available rather than running Stockfish from scratch. The export is released under CC0, which permits unrestricted research, redistribution, and modification. Raw record. Lichess game is sequence of half-moves recorded in PGN, plus per-game metadata (the two players Lichess handles, their ELO ratings at the time of the game, time control, opening ECO code, and final outcome). For each half-move we extract the position before the move in FEN notation, the players actual move in UCI, and engine-derived quality features for that move: the engine top-k move list with their centipawn evaluations, the players centipawn loss for the played move, binary is_best_move flag from the engine ranking, the index of the played move within the engine top-k list, and the move-index within the game (used downstream to bucket positions by phase). The fields kept in each per-position record are therefore: player_handle, player_elo, time_control, game_outcome, move_idx, fen_before, player_uci, engine_top_k, cp_loss, is_best_move, and player_move_rank. We discard pre-move clock times, evaluation comments embedded in the PGN, and game-chat fields. Positions are bucketed by phase into very-early opening (move_idx < 10), opening (move_idx [10, 19]), middlegame ([20, 39]), and endgame ( 40). Single-turn record format Si = {(x, m)}. The single-turn input is templated player-context prompt followed by the FEN of position and request for the next move in UCI. The player-context block is fully derivable from the players prior games on Lichess and contains: basic profile (recent win rate, best-move accuracy, average centipawn loss), coarse style label (offensive / balanced / defensive) plus offensive-move and defensive-move rates, per-piece usage rates, recent-history features (last three game results, current best-move streak by player and opponent, recent captures gained and lost), an opening-move-tendency line for early-game positions (move_idx 10), and top-5 Maia2-derived candidate-move list with per-move probabilities. For the closed-source LLM baselines we omit the Maia2-derived candidate-move list, so their scores reflect only their own student modeling and are not influenced by Maia2s predictions. Multi-turn records are drawn from positions outside the very-early opening (move_idx 10), because an opening move reflects players repertoire and preparation, where there is no single move to correct toward. First, training and evaluation share the same form: the simulator is trained on multiple-choice records at both turns, and decoding letter at evaluation matches the training distribution rather than crossing free-text / categorical boundary that would penalize the simulator for an artifact of formatting. Second, 30 StudentSim: Training LLM-based Student Simulators the candidate set is constructed from the same empirical other-student answer pool used at the student turn, so the comparison is held against the answers students do actually give on this problem; the canonical corrected answer competes against three real alternative forms rather than against random distractors, and the metric rewards simulator that resolves to the corrected form among realistic competitors. We considered free-text exact match against and rejected it because string normalization absorbs or fails to absorb form differences (e.g., 0.5 versus .5 versus 1/2) inconsistently across simulators, and that surface-form noise dominates the per-record signal under exact match; the four-way form with empirical distractors converts surface-form variation into the candidate set itself and lets the metric score whether the simulator selects the corrected canonical letter among the realistic alternatives. Reproducibility note: bf16 nondeterminism on small samples. On the open-source per-student simulator (LoRA over bf16 Qwen3-4B-Instruct base), greedy single-token decoding on borderline-logit records can flip across runs because of nondeterministic bf16 accumulation. The effect is per-record and averages out at scale: on 315-record cap-7 subsample of the math evaluation set the same checkpoint scored = 0.565 on first pass and = 0.952 on re-run, while on the full 879-record no-cap evaluation set the population mean is stable across re-runs at the headline value reported in Table 3. The closed-source baselines (GPT-4o, GPT-5.4) are queried with API temperature 0 and are much less sensitive to within-checkpoint jitter. For faithful comparison the headline math number is reported on the full no-cap 879-record set; we recommend reproducing on the same set rather than on downsample. sections.title: D Training Pipeline Ablations and Parameter Sweeps
sections.content: This appendix reports the chess-domain sweeps that set the default training recipe for the reference simulators, together with robustness check on the pooled two-turn fraction. We run these sweeps only in chess. Chess is the most challenging of the three domains to retrain end-to-end (since LLMs are less familiar with playing chess than learning second-language or doing mathematics), and it uses the same two training stages and the same guidance-conditioning mechanism as the other two domains. We then transfer the resulting recipe to second-language English writing and to mathematics without per-knob retuning. This appendix therefore establishes default recipe, not claim that each knob has the same optimum in every domain. We first ablate the main pipeline choice of cross-student pooling in Stage 1, then examine three recipe settings: i) input modality (text vs. vision), ii) the fraction of guidance data in pooled-training, and iii) the composition of the guidance-mode mix. We report two summaries. on chess is the population mean of the per-student behavioral-fidelity score, measured on held-out positions on randomly selected 3 students. on chess is the Turn-2 move accuracy on held-out evaluation set of guided interactions. The board positions in this evaluation set are held out from both training stages, and the set covers all four chess guidance modes (error remediation, Socratic, strategic, comparative) with an equal number of positions per mode. The equal-count construction ensures that reflects overall guidance responsiveness rather than capability on whichever mode happens to be most represented in evaluation, and it also makes per-mode breakdowns directly comparable. Both metrics are defined formally in Section 5.2 and Section 5.3. Each sweep is evaluated as matched comparison within its own run configuration and student subset, so rows inside table are directly comparable, while rows from different tables come from separate ablation runs. D.1 What Stage-1 Pooling Contributes This ablation asks what the pooled Stage-1 corpus contributes in the main pipeline, holding the optimization budget fixed. In the reference condition, Stage 1 trains on 100,000 chess records pooled from 100 players, giving 391 optimizer steps at effective batch 256. In the matched ablation, Stage 1 instead trains on one players own 1,000 records repeated 100 times, which produces the same 391 optimizer steps under the same effective batch, LoRA rank and scaling, learning rates, warmup, and seed. Stage 2 is identical in both conditions: the model is specialized on that players own 1,000 records for 12 optimizer steps. This construction holds the update budget fixed and changes only the number of distinct students represented in Stage 1. We evaluate on three randomly sampled players. Table 11 Ablation of cross-student pooling in chess Stage 1. The reference arm uses the default pooled Stage-1 corpus of 100,000 records from 100 players. The matched ablation replaces this with one players own 1,000 records repeated 100 times, which preserves the Stage-1 optimizer budget (391 steps) and all training hyperparameters. Both arms then run the same Stage-2 specialization on that players own 1,000 records (12 steps). Results are averaged over three ramdomly sampled players. Stage-1 corpus pooled across 100 players (default) one players own records, repeated 0.5131 0.4602 0.9003 0.8276 Cross-student pooling is what the pooled stage contributes. In Table 11, the reference arm reaches = 0.5131 and = 0.9003, while the repeated-single-student arm reaches = 0.4602 and = 0.8276. The same pattern holds for each player individually: fidelity drops from 0.4558 to 0.3992, from 0.4660 to 0.4186, and from 0.6174 to 0.5628, while responsiveness drops from 0.9093 to 0.8363, from 0.8928 to 0.8238, and from 0.8990 to 0.8228. With Stage-1 and Stage-2 step counts, schedules, and data volume matched, the gain in the reference arm comes from the Stage-1 corpus spanning many students. Repeating one players limited records for the same number of updates does not reproduce the effect of pooling across students. 32 StudentSim: Training LLM-based Student Simulators D.2 Input Modality: Text vs. Vision Chess is one of the three domains where non-textual encoding of the students working state is available: the board position can be rendered as an image and consumed by vision-language base. We compared the text-only recipe (Qwen3-4B-Instruct, FEN plus features rendered as string) against matched vision-language recipe (Qwen3-VL-4BInstruct, 400 400 board image plus the same text features), keeping every other hyperparameter fixed at the chess defaults. Table 12 Modality sweep on chess. The board image adds 0.001 to and requires vision tower in the training loop; the two arms are matched on effective batch size. Modality training cost (relative) text-only (Qwen3-4B-Instruct) vision-language (Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct) 0.536 0. 1.0 2.0 Table 12 shows that the visual board does not improve in any meaningful sense. The textual board encoding (FEN plus the candidate-move and history features described in Section 4) already specifies the full game state relevant to move selection, so the rendered image adds little new information beyond what the text encoding already carries. We therefore use the text-only recipe in every domain. The other two domains are already text-native, so we do not repeat the modality sweep there. D.3 Robustness to the Pooled Two-Turn Fraction The pooled-training mix contains both single-turn samples (board move) and two-turn samples (board move; AI tutor guidance revised move). The mixing ratio ρ controls the fraction of two-turn samples in the pooled stage. We fix ρ = 0.2 in all production runs, and the sweep below checks whether the papers conclusions depend on that setting. Table 13 Multi-turn mixing-ratio sweep on chess (sequential sampler, fixed Turn-2 suffix). Adding any nonzero amount of guidance data lifts from 0.17 to above 0.80. From there stays on plateau, and is unaffected by ρ within 0.004. The production setting ρ = 0.20 sits inside the plateau. multi-turn ratio ρ R vs. ρ = 0 0.000 (single-turn only) 0.025 0.05 0.10 0.20 (default) 0.40 0.80 0.490 0.489 0.488 0.489 0.487 0.491 0.487 0.167 0.826 0.849 0.816 0.859 0.878 0.857 n/a +0.659 +0.682 +0.649 +0.692 +0.711 +0. Two facts stand out. First, is essentially invariant in ρ across the full range, so fidelity is stable under the Stage-1 multi-turn mixing ratio and no fidelity result hinges on this setting. Second, reaches its high-value regime as soon as any guidance data is present and stays there, so the guidance results at ρ = 0.2 sit well inside plateau. That plateau is not automatic: without fixed Turn-2 suffix that re-asks for the updated move, some runs at intermediate ρ fail on error remediation by stopping after the reasoning trace instead of emitting move. Pairing sequential sampling with the Turn-2 suffix removes that failure mode and produces the wide plateau in Table 13. D.4 Guidance-Mode Composition Chess uses four guidance modes (Section 5.3): error remediation (the tutor diagnoses the weakness in the students move, then motivates the correct answer with concrete consequences or alternative candidates), strategic (the tutor states plan such as activate the king-side rook), comparative (the tutor contrasts other stronger candidate moves), and Socratic (the tutor asks question that prompts the student to derive the move themselves, e.g. what is Black threatening on the next move?). We include error remediation because direct correction is one end of the assistance dilemma [Koedinger and Aleven, 2007]: when student is stuck or repeatedly failing, the appropriate tutor action is to supply the move and the reason for it, and faithful simulator population has to cover that end of the spectrum as well. We include the Socratic mode to represent guided discovery at the indirect end of the tutoring spectrum, where the 33 StudentSim: Training LLM-based Student Simulators tutor prompts the student to resolve the correction. Because the tutor does not state which move to play, this mode is demanding for the simulator, which must combine the students characteristic style with the tutors reasoning prompt. Mixing four modes during pooled-training is meant to prevent the simulator from collapsing onto whichever mode is easiest. We swept the per-mode composition at fixed ρ = 0.2 in three ways: i) leave-one-out, dropping each mode in turn, ii) single-mode training, keeping only one mode, and iii) Socratic weight scaling, multiplying the Socratic modes weight while keeping the others at 1. Table 14, Table 15, and Table 16 report broken down by evaluation mode. Table 14 Leave-one-out sweep on chess. Each row drops one guidance mode from the pooled-training mix and evaluates on all four modes. Even one-mode training reaches [0.72, 0.80], against 0.836 for the four-mode default. Comparative-only transfers best to the other three modes, and error-remediation-only transfers worst. training mode (single mode at full weight) error rem. strategic comparative Socratic all four (uniform default, ref) comparative only strategic only Socratic only error remediation only 0.836 0.798 0.790 0.769 0.720 0.962 0.926 0.859 0.864 0.898 0.880 0.850 0.857 0.816 0.751 0.890 0.865 0.883 0.878 0.781 0.611 0.552 0.562 0.519 0.449 Table 16 Weight-scaling sweep on chess: scaling the Socratic mode while keeping the other three at 1. Multiplying the Socratic weight raises the Socratic per-mode score from 0.611 to 0.670 (+5.9 pp at 4). The other three modes shift by few points at the strongest setting, and overall is close to flat. training mix (weights err:strat:comp:soc) error rem. strategic comparative Socratic 1:1:1:1 (uniform default) 1:1:1:2 (boost Socratic 2) 1:1:1:4 (boost Socratic 4) 0.836 0.842 0. 0.962 0.972 0.924 0.880 0.875 0.864 0.890 0.884 0.904 0.611 0.635 0.670 Three findings come out of this chess composition sweep. Modes partly substitute for one another during pooled-training. In Table 14, removing error remediation, comparative, or Socratic does not lower that modes evaluation score, and in two of those three cases the score on the dropped mode actually rises. The most extreme case is comparative: removing it from training raises the comparative evaluation score from 0.890 to 0.934. The four guidance modes share enough underlying structure (extracting chess move that is consistent with both the students prior and the AI tutors pedagogical signal) that training on three of them transfers to the fourth. Strategic is the one exception: its removal lowers overall R, which suggests that strategic carries pedagogical signal the other three modes do not fully cover. model trained on one mode still answers the other three. Table 15 pushes the substitutability claim further: training the pooled-training mix on single guidance mode and evaluating on all four still gives [0.72, 0.80], compared with 0.836 for the four-mode default. The transfer is asymmetric. Comparative-only training transfers best (overall = 0.798), consistent with comparative being the most redundant mode in the leave-one-out sweep. Error-remediationonly training transfers worst (overall = 0.720). This mode delivers full diagnosis of the mistake together with the correction and its rationale, and naming the move comes with that direct-correction role; model trained on it alone can settle for copying the named move, which does not carry over to the other three modes, where the tutor does not 34 StudentSim: Training LLM-based Student Simulators state which move to play. The Socratic per-mode score also stays low ( 0.56) in every single-mode row, so Socratic capability is the hardest piece to acquire by transfer alone and benefits most from being explicitly represented in the training mix. Per-mode capability is controllable through training-data weights. In Table 16, scaling the Socratic weight scales the Socratic per-mode score in graded way, with the other three modes shifting by few points at the strongest setting. The per-mode weighting handle is useful when downstream experiment needs different per-mode profile: simulator that is especially responsive to Socratic guidance, or that under-responds to it to model student who ignores reasoning prompts, can be produced by adjusting the pooled-training mix rather than by adding new training procedures or new objectives. The reference simulators reported in the main paper use the uniform 1:1:1:1 default; the weight-scaling result is recorded here only to document that the per-mode profile can be adjusted predictably.

sections.title: E Training and Experimental Details
sections.content: This appendix records the hyperparameters and infrastructure that produced every checkpoint and metric reported in Section 5.2, Section 5.3, and Section 6. Data sources, training-instance formats, and corpus statistics are in Appendix B; metric definitions are in Appendix C; sweep results that motivated the recipe are in Appendix D. reader who reproduces the source corpora and follows the values in the tables below should be able to retrain the full reference family and rerun every evaluation reported in the main paper. The base model in all three domains is Qwen3-4B-Instruct, specifically the Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 release [Yang et al., 2025]. Training is in bf16 on single 8 A100 (40 GB) node using ms-swift [Zhao et al., 2025]. Both stages train LoRA adapters [Hu et al., 2021]; Stage 1 trains fresh LoRA on the pooled-training corpus, and Stage 2 loads the Stage-1 adapter and continues training that adapter on one students records with smaller learning rate. Stage 2 therefore inherits the Stage-1 LoRA architecture (rank, α, dropout, target modules) in all three domains. The single random seed is the ms-swift trainer default (42) for optimizer state and dataloader shuffling, with separate seed (65) for the data sampler that constructs the per-domain training-instance pool. Two-stage training and shared design. The two-stage design separates Stage-1 pooled training phase that pools records across large student set from Stage-2 specialization phase that adapts the resulting LoRA adapter to one students records. The two stages share the base model (Qwen3-4B-Instruct), LoRA rank, α, dropout, target modules, optimizer (AdamW with β = (0.9, 0.95)), bf16 precision with gradient checkpointing, weight decay, gradient-norm clip, max sequence length, loss masking, trainer seed, and data-sampler seed; they differ only in learning rate, schedule, warmup length, and the per-domain values of corpus size, effective batch, and optimization length. Within each stage we keep single shared configuration across chess, L2, and math; the per-domain values that differ (Table 18 and Table 20) are dictated by per-domain dataset scale, not tuned for any single benchmark. Every deviation from the shared configuration is enumerated in Section E.2. E.1 Stage 1 Hyperparameters Stage 1 trains one domain-specific LoRA on the pooled-training corpus described in Appendix B, mixing single-turn and multi-turn records at fixed multi-turn ratio of ρ = 0.20 in all three domains; Appendix D.3 shows that the results do not depend on this setting.
